Total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) consists of the Corporation's Tier 1 capital and eligible long-term debt issued directly by the Corporation.
Eligible long-term debt for TLAC ratios is comprised of unsecured debt that has a remaining maturity of at least one year and satisfies additional requirements as prescribed in the TLAC final rule.

comparisons.peer_topic: TLAC and LTD Regulatory Requirements for U.S. GSIBs
comparisons.peer_summary: U.S. Global Systemically Important Banks (GSIBs) must maintain minimum levels of Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) and eligible Long-Term Debt (LTD) based on consolidated risk-weighted assets and total leverage exposure. The purpose of these requirements is to ensure the orderly resolution of these institutions under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act, with specific company amounts detailed in the Capital Resources section.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Citi disclose that U.S. GSIBs are required to maintain minimum levels of TLAC and eligible LTD to ensure orderly resolution. JPMorgan specifically notes the August 2023 regulatory proposal to expand these requirements to non-GSIBs with over $100 billion in assets and reduce the count of short-maturity LTD, whereas Citi describes the current baseline requirements based on risk-weighted assets and total leverage exposure without mentioning the specific expansion proposal to non-GSIBs.

sentences.text: Additionally, in August 2023, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC and the OCC released a proposal to expand the eligible long-term debt ("eligible LTD") and clean holding company requirements under the existing total loss-absorbing capacity ("TLAC") rule to apply to non-GSIB banks with $100 billion or more in total consolidated assets.

The proposal would also reduce the amount of LTD with remaining maturities of less than two years that count towards a U.S. GSIB's TLAC requirement and expand the existing capital deduction framework for LTD issued by GSIBs to include LTD issued by non-GSIB banks subject to the LTD requirements.
U.S. GSIBs are required to maintain minimum levels of TLAC and eligible LTD, each set by reference to the GSIB's consolidated risk-weighted assets (RWA) and total leverage exposure.
The intended purpose of the requirements is to facilitate the orderly resolution of U.S. GSIBs under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act.

comparisons.peer_topic: Composition of TLAC and Eligible Debt
comparisons.peer_summary: TLAC includes common and preferred stock and eligible long-term debt issued by Group Inc., defined as unsecured debt with at least one year maturity and other requirements, while external long-term debt consists of eligible debt subject to a haircut if due between one and two years.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs discuss the composition of eligible long-term debt within the TLAC framework. JPMorgan highlights a proposed rule change that would reduce the amount of LTD with remaining maturities of less than two years counting towards TLAC. Goldman Sachs currently defines eligible long-term debt as unsecured debt with a remaining maturity of at least one year and notes that external long-term debt is subject to a haircut if due between one and two years, reflecting the current treatment of short-maturity debt that JPMorgan identifies as a target for regulatory change.

comparisons.peer_topic: TLAC and LTD Ratio Definitions and Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: Required TLAC ratios include applicable buffers and consist of CET1 capital, Additional Tier 1 capital (excluding noncontrolling interests), and eligible LTD, with LTD reduced by 50% for unpaid principal due in one to two years. Clean holding company requirements prohibit covered BHCs from incurring external debt with maturities less than one year and cap certain other external liabilities at 5% of outstanding external TLAC, while capital deductions apply for investments in unsecured debt instruments issued by the Parent Company or other G-SIBs.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley discuss the interaction between TLAC requirements and clean holding company rules, specifically regarding short-term debt. JPMorgan's disclosure focuses on a proposal to reduce the LTD with maturities of less than two years counting towards TLAC. Morgan Stanley details the current 'clean holding company requirements' which prohibit external debt with an original maturity of less than one year and reduce the count of LTD by 50% for amounts due in more than one but less than two years, illustrating the existing mechanics of the short-maturity LTD treatment that JPMorgan notes is being proposed for further reduction/expansion.

sentences.text: Additionally, in August 2023, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC and the OCC released a proposal to expand the eligible long-term debt ("eligible LTD") and clean holding company requirements under the existing total loss-absorbing capacity ("TLAC") rule to apply to non-GSIB banks with $100 billion or more in total consolidated assets.

The proposal would also reduce the amount of LTD with remaining maturities of less than two years that count towards a U.S. GSIB's TLAC requirement and expand the existing capital deduction framework for LTD issued by GSIBs to include LTD issued by non-GSIB banks subject to the LTD requirements.
